title: Find Where a Linked-List Cycle Begins
statement:
Detecting that a linked list loops is the easy question. The follow-up is the
one interviewers actually ask: **which node does the loop start at?** -- in
O(1) extra memory.

## The type

```
struct ListNode
{
    int val;
    ListNode* next;
};
```

## Your function

```
const ListNode* CycleStart(const ListNode* head);
```

If the list ends in `nullptr`, return `nullptr`. Otherwise, some node's `next`
points back to an earlier node (or to itself): return **that earlier node**, the
first node that is part of the cycle when walking from `head`.

```
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5
          ^         |
          +---------+        CycleStart returns the node holding 3
```

`head` may be `nullptr`; a single node may point to itself.

## Watch out

- **Where the slow and fast pointers meet is *not* the start of the cycle.**
  It is some node inside it. A solution that returns the meeting point is
  correct for "is there a cycle?" and wrong for this question.
- **Phase two:** once they meet, reset one pointer to `head` and advance
  *both* one step at a time; they next meet exactly at the start of the
  cycle. (The distance from `head` to the start equals the distance from the
  meeting point to the start, going round the loop.)
- **Guard the fast pointer:** it moves two steps, so check both `fast` and
  `fast->next` for `nullptr` before dereferencing -- an acyclic list ends
  there.
- **Start both pointers at `head`, and test for a meeting *after* moving.**
  Testing before the first move reports a "cycle" in every list.
- An O(n) memory solution (a set of visited nodes) also passes; the
  constant-memory version is what the interviewer is waiting for.

a single node pointing at itself
tests.description: head->next == head: the cycle starts at the head.
